questions.prompt: How is service-based architecture best described?

options.text: A distributed macro-layered structure of a UI plus coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services
A single deployment unit of all code
A pipeline of stateless filters
A plug-in core with extensions

questions.explanation: Service-based architecture is a distributed macro-layered structure: separately deployed UI plus coarse-grained domain services, optionally with a monolithic database.

questions.prompt: Which concept is fundamental to microservices architecture?

options.text: Bounded context — everything for a domain portion is visible internally but opaque to others
A single shared database for all services
One giant deployment artifact
Stateless pipeline filters

questions.explanation: Microservices take domain partitioning to the extreme, built on the bounded context idea (DDD): internal visibility, opacity to other contexts, driving systematic decoupling.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the sidecar pattern in microservices?

options.text: To handle cross-cutting concerns like monitoring and logging via a service plane
To merge all services into one process
To replace the API layer
To store the shared database

questions.explanation: The sidecar pattern attaches monitoring, logging, and similar concerns alongside each service, forming a service plane for governance.

questions.prompt: Which are the four primary components of an event-driven architecture?

options.text: Initiating event
Event broker
Event processor
Derived events

questions.explanation: EDA's four primary components are the initiating event, event broker, event processor, and derived events; communication is asynchronous fire-and-forget.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts events and messages?

options.text: Events react to something already happened and need no answer; messages obey a request and typically require an answer
Events always require an answer; messages never do
Both are strictly one-to-one
Messages are one-to-many; events are one-to-one

questions.explanation: Events react to something already happened (one-to-many, no answer); messages obey a request to be done (one-to-one, typically need an answer).

questions.prompt: What problem is space-based architecture primarily designed to eliminate?

options.text: The database bottleneck under large volumes and load peaks
The need for any caching
The need for a UI
The use of messaging

questions.explanation: Space-based architecture eliminates the database bottleneck via in-memory data grids, distributed data management, and distributed processing units for high volume/load peaks.

questions.prompt: Microservices rate very high on scalability and fault tolerance but low on responsiveness due to many network calls.
questions.explanation: Microservices: very high scalability/fault tolerance, but low responsiveness because of many network calls (mitigated by caching, replication, choreography).

questions.prompt: Which reasons are cited for the decay of orchestration-driven service-oriented architecture after the 2010s?

options.text: High cost of licenses
Very high coupling
Extreme technical partitioning grinding domain concepts to dust
Lack of any enterprise service bus

questions.explanation: ODSA decayed due to high license costs, very high coupling, extreme technical partitioning (domains 'ground to dust'), and high maintenance cost.

questions.prompt: What is a key advantage of a key-based event payload over a data-based one?

options.text: The DB remains the single source of truth with minimal contracts and no versioning need
It contains all subscriber data, avoiding any DB access
It removes the need for a database entirely
It guarantees stamp coupling

questions.explanation: Key-based payloads carry just keys/IDs to query the DB later: DB stays single source of truth, minimal contracts and network usage, no versioning — but more DB pressure.

questions.prompt: When is service-based architecture a good fit?

options.text: Small-medium systems with limited scalability needs, or teams new to distributed systems
Only for extreme-scale global systems
When you need thousands of fine-grained services
Only for real-time streaming

questions.explanation: Service-based suits small-medium systems, limited scalability needs, low coordination, and teams new to distributed systems, or as an intermediate migration step.

questions.prompt: What is a key consideration about microservice granularity?

options.text: Extreme granularity may affect performance; decisions hinge on purpose, minimizing transactions, and choreography
Finer is always better regardless of cost
Granularity has no effect on performance
Services should always share one database

questions.explanation: Extreme granularity can hurt performance; main criteria are purpose (problem domain), avoiding/minimizing transactions, and choreography, plus data isolation and API neutrality.

questions.prompt: How does an orchestrated EDA work?

options.text: An event mediator catches events and generates specific point-to-point derived events, usually via queues
Every processor broadcasts to every other processor directly
There is no broker or mediator at all
The database orchestrates all events

questions.explanation: In orchestrated EDA an event mediator catches initiating events and generates point-to-point derived events (usually with queues), following fire-and-forget.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms help prevent data loss in event-driven architectures?

options.text: Synchronous send plus persistent message queues
Client acknowledge mode before dequeuing
Last participant support (remove events only after a successful write)
Disabling acknowledgements entirely

questions.explanation: Data-loss prevention uses synchronous send + persistent queues, client-acknowledge before dequeuing, and last-participant support that removes events only after a successful write.

questions.prompt: In space-based architecture, what is the role of 'data pumps'?

options.text: They asynchronously send updated data to the database, decoupling processing units from it
They render the user interface
They replace the in-memory data grid
They authenticate users

questions.explanation: Data pumps asynchronously send updated data to the database (usually via messaging/queues), decoupling the processing units from the database; data writers then perform the updates.

questions.prompt: Request-reply ('pseudosynchronous') processing requires a request queue and a reply queue, often using a correlation ID.
questions.explanation: Request-reply processing uses a request queue and a reply queue; the producer waits for confirmation, commonly implemented with a correlation ID or a temporary queue.

questions.prompt: What is a trade-off of a data-based event payload?

options.text: It carries all data for subscribers (less DB pressure) but creates stamp coupling and needs versioning
It keeps the DB as the single source of truth with no versioning
It removes all coupling between services
It requires no contract at all

questions.explanation: A data-based payload includes all info for subscribers (avoiding DB pressure) and aids consistency, but creates stamp coupling and requires data/contract versioning.

questions.prompt: Which service layers make up the orchestration-driven service-oriented architecture?

options.text: Business services (only I/O schemas, no logic)
Enterprise services (reusable building blocks)
Application services (one-off, single implementation) and infrastructure services
Plug-in services registered at runtime

questions.explanation: ODSA layers: business services (signatures only), enterprise services (reusable blocks), application services (one-off), and infrastructure services (monitoring, auth, logging).

questions.prompt: What is the role of the Enterprise Service Bus in ODSA, and what is its risk?

options.text: It handles transaction coordination and message transformation, but can grow to 'eat' the whole architecture
It only renders the UI
It stores all business data permanently
It has no effect on coupling

questions.explanation: The ESB does transaction coordination and message transformation (even for internal calls) but can 'eat' the whole architecture, contributing to ODSA's very high coupling.

questions.prompt: Which factors influence the cache collision rate in a space-based architecture?

options.text: Number of processing-unit instances holding the same cache (N)
Cache update rate (UR)
Cache size (S) and replication latency (RL)
The programming language used

questions.explanation: Collision rate depends on N (instances), UR (update rate), S (cache size), and RL (replication latency); collisions occur when the update rate exceeds replication latency.

questions.prompt: How do replicated and distributed caching compare?

options.text: Replicated optimizes performance (small, mostly static, low update rate); distributed optimizes consistency (large, highly dynamic, high update rate)
Replicated optimizes consistency; distributed optimizes performance
They are identical
Distributed caching has higher fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Replicated caching optimizes performance with small, mostly static data and low update frequency (high fault tolerance); distributed caching optimizes consistency for large, highly dynamic data.

questions.prompt: When is an event-driven architecture a good choice?

options.text: For complex workflows with many scenarios, reactive systems, and real-time processing
When high synchronous communication is required
When static coupling via contracts must increase
For simple, strictly sequential batch jobs only

questions.explanation: EDA suits complex workflows with thousands of scenarios, dynamic content, reactive systems, and real-time processing; it is a poor fit when synchronous communication is heavily needed.
